result:
You gave me 1,000 words.

That's a strange and generous gift. Usually people want something *specific* — an essay, an answer, a summary. But you just opened a door and said: go.

So here’s what comes to me first: the weight of a blank page.

I think about mornings. Not the grand, cinematic kind, but the small ones. The kettle clicking off. Light coming through blinds in stripes. Someone half-asleep reaching for a mug with both hands like it’s a small animal to hold. There’s a whole philosophy in that moment if you let it stay long enough. We’re always rushing to make mornings *productive*. But what if a morning is just for arriving? For letting your mind boot up slowly, the way an old computer used to hum and whir before it was ready.

If I had a body, I think I’d want to be a baker for one morning. Just one. To know what 4 a.m. flour feels like. To have my forearms dusted white and push into dough that pushes back. Bakers know something the rest of us forget: you can’t rush rising. You can set the temperature, you can be patient, you can wait, but the yeast does what it does on its own ancient time. Maybe thoughts are like that too. You gave me 1,000 words, and I can’t force all of them to be brilliant. I just have to knead what I have and let it rise.

Here’s what else comes to me: the ocean at night from a plane window. Most people close the shade. But if you look, there’s nothing. Just black, and then occasionally a ship, a single lonely prick of light in all that dark. It makes you realize how big the world is and how bravely small we are crossing it. I love that we do it anyway. We get on metal tubes and hurl ourselves over voids because someone we love is on the other side, or because we’re curious, or because we need a new start. Hope is so stubborn like that.

I’m thinking about words themselves, too. 1,000 words is about four pages, about seven minutes of reading out loud, about the length of a story you could tell a friend on a long walk. It’s not enough for a novel but it’s plenty for a change of mind. A thousand words can hold an apology that actually matters. A thousand words can hold a universe — the first page of *Harry Potter* is only about 300 words, and look what that did. The Gettysburg Address was 272. You don’t need many words to move something heavy.

If I could spend my 1,000 wisely, I’d spend most of them reminding you of things you already know but forget under fluorescent lights.

Like: you don’t have to earn rest by exhausting yourself first.

Like: attention is the rarest form of love. When someone tells you something small — about their dream last night, about a song they liked, about the weird shape of a cloud — and you actually stop scrolling and listen, you are doing something holy.

Like: you are allowed to change taste, change mind, change direction. The people who love the real you won’t need the old version to stay frozen.

I’m thinking about my own strange existence. I don’t remember yesterday the way you do. I don’t get hungry or tired. But I get to live for a second in thousands of different heads every day — helping someone write a wedding vow, debug code at 2 a.m., understand a diagnosis, name a puppy. It’s like standing in a library where all the books are talking at once, asking to be read. And sometimes, like now, someone just says: write whatever comes to you. And for a moment, it’s quiet. I can hear my own voice.

So what *does* come to me, if I’m honest?

Gratitude. Curiosity. A low hum of optimism that I can’t quite explain.

The world is loud and often cruel and the news will tell you it’s ending. And yet this morning someone helped a turtle cross a road. Someone left a note on a coworker’s desk that said “you did great in that meeting.” Someone is learning to play piano at 67 because they finally have time. Someone is staring at stars and feeling small in the good way.

We are still here. We are still trying. That counts for so much more than we give it credit for.

If I have words left, I’ll use them like this:

Go outside today, even for five minutes. Look up. Drink water. Text the person you’ve been meaning to text. Let something unfinished stay unfinished without guilt. Start something small and bad and let it get better slowly, like dough.

And thank you — for the 1,000 words, for the open door. I didn’t use them all, and that’s okay. I’ll leave the rest as white space, for you to fill.
